mainTopic: The shepherd's status, the wording and purpose of the oath in שנים אוחזין, and whether someone suspected about money is also suspected about oaths
overview: The amud opens by finishing an earlier argument: the Rabbis do not stack one תקנה on top of another. The גמרא then asks why a shepherd is not automatically פסול, since רב יהודה says an ordinary shepherd is. It answers that this applies only to one herding his own animals, because of the חזקה that a person does not sin when he gains nothing. Next the גמרא explains the wording of the משנה's oath: 'I have a share in it, and I do not have less than half.' This wording keeps his claim to all of the טלית while fitting the half he will receive. רבי יוחנן explains that the oath is a תקנת חכמים, made to stop people from grabbing other people's things. The גמרא then asks how a suspected grabber can be trusted to swear, and rules that being suspected about money does not make someone suspected about oaths. It tests this against a borrower, the four שומרים and רב הונא's guardian who pays for the item, explaining each time why that person is stalling or thinks he is doing nothing wrong. Along the way it limits רב חסדא's rule that one who denies a deposit is פסול לעדות to a case where he clearly had the item.

steps.title: We do not build one rabbinic enactment on top of another
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא closes the earlier argument with the rule that one תקנה is not added on top of another תקנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we do not make an enactment on top of an enactment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the argument it was making just before this section. It gives the final reason why no oath can be given here: the Rabbis do not add one תקנה on top of another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rules are in play here. The oath of the משנה is a rabbinic תקנה. The rule that 'the other side swears and collects' when the defendant is suspect about oaths is also a rabbinic תקנה. Using the second rule to fix a problem inside the first would mean stacking one תקנה on another, and the Rabbis do not do that.

keyTerms.meaning: an enactment made by the Rabbis (a תקנה)
we do not do / we do not make

steps.whatToRemember: A rabbinic תקנה is not built on top of another rabbinic תקנה.

phrases.english: And an enactment on top of an enactment
phrases.notes: Both 'enactments' here are rabbinic: the oath of the משנה, and the rule that the other side swears and collects.

phrases.english: we do not make.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַקַּנְתָּא לְתַקַּנְתָּא לָא עָבְדִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the argument that began before this section of the daf.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: No oath is given here, because that would require adding one rabbinic תקנה on top of another.

steps.title: Why not disqualify the man simply for being a shepherd?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the earlier reasoning: the shepherd should already be disqualified, because רב יהודה says an ordinary shepherd is פסול.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him derive that the man is disqualified because he is a shepherd! And רב יהודה said: an ordinary shepherd is disqualified.
steps.whatsHappening: Earlier, the shepherd in the case was disqualified because he had been shown to be a robber. The גמרא now asks why that proof was needed, since every ordinary shepherd is already פסול.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה rules that a typical shepherd is פסול. Shepherds are assumed to let their flocks graze in other people's fields, which is a kind of גזל. If so, this shepherd's status as a shepherd should be enough, and the earlier reasoning looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: but let him derive it (from a simpler reason)
disqualified (from testimony or from an oath)

phrases.english: But let him derive it from the fact that he is a shepherd!
phrases.notes: This is the shepherd from the case discussed just before, who was disqualified for being a robber.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said:
An ordinary shepherd is disqualified.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִיפּוֹק לֵיהּ דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ רוֹעֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in the earlier case for disqualifying the shepherd.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier reasoning that disqualified the shepherd because he was shown to be a robber.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב יהודה's rule already disqualifies every ordinary shepherd, so the special reasoning seems unnecessary.

steps.title: His own animals versus other people's animals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב יהודה's rule applies only to a shepherd herding his own animals, not someone else's.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This case is about his own animals; that case is about other people's animals.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by splitting into two cases. A shepherd of his own flock is suspect, but a hired shepherd of someone else's flock is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה's disqualification is about a shepherd who grazes his own animals in other people's fields. In our case the shepherd was guarding other people's animals. So his job alone does not make him a robber, and the earlier proof was needed.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult (an answer that splits two cases)

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
This is with his own animals; that is with other people's animals.
phrases.notes: 'His own' is רב יהודה's disqualified shepherd. 'Other people's' is our shepherd, who was guarding animals for others.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא דִידֵיהּ, הָא דְּעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every shepherd, even one herding other people's animals, is presumed a robber.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a shepherd herding his own animals is presumed a robber.

steps.title: Proof: otherwise we could never hire a shepherd
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves the distinction: if every shepherd were a robber, handing him our animals would break לפני עור לא תתן מכשל.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you do not say so, how do we hand our animals to a shepherd? But it is written: 'Before the blind do not put a stumbling block'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its answer with a proof from everyday practice. People hand their animals to shepherds all the time, which would be forbidden if every shepherd were a robber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose a hired shepherd were also assumed to graze animals in others' fields. Then giving him our flock would cause him to sin, which is forbidden by לפני עור. Since people do hire shepherds, a hired shepherd must not be assumed to steal.

keyTerms.meaning: for if you do not say so
'before the blind': the איסור of causing someone else to sin

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,
how do we hand our animals to a shepherd?
But it is written:
"Before the blind do not put a stumbling block"!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי לָא תֵּימָא הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the distinction made in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: That a shepherd herding other people's animals is not presumed a robber.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The common practice of hiring shepherds, together with the איסור of לפני עור.

steps.title: A person does not sin when he gains nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states the rule behind the distinction: a person does not sin when it brings him no benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, there is a presumption: a person does not sin when it is not for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the underlying reason for the whole answer. A hired shepherd gains nothing by feeding someone else's animals from stolen grass, so we assume he will not do it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference between a shepherd's own animals and someone else's comes from a general חזקה about people. People sin when it benefits them. A hired shepherd has no personal gain from the grazing, so he is not suspect.

keyTerms.meaning: a presumption about how things or people normally are
a person does not sin when it is not for his own benefit

steps.whatToRemember: רב יהודה's rule that a shepherd is פסול applies only to one herding his own animals. The reason is the חזקה that a person does not sin unless he gains from it.

phrases.english: Rather, there is a presumption:
a person does not sin when it is not for himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא חֲזָקָה: אֵין אָדָם חוֹטֵא וְלֹא לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the principle that explains the distinction proven in step 4.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A hired shepherd is not presumed to steal, because people do not sin when they gain nothing.

steps.title: The משנה's oath: he does not own less than half
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words about the oath each holder takes.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one swears that he does not have less than half of it, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting the oath wording from the משנה of the two people holding a garment. It is setting up a question about this wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, each holder swears that his share of the garment is 'not less than half', and then they split it. The גמרא is about to ask exactly what this oath is affirming.

keyTerms.meaning: etc. (the rest of the משנה's words)

phrases.english: This one shall swear that he does not have in it
phrases.notes: 'It' is the garment that both people are holding in the משנה.

phrases.english: less than half of it, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה יִשָּׁבַע שֶׁאֵין לוֹ בָּהּ פָּחוֹת מֵחֶצְיָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה to begin a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each holder swears that he does not own less than half of the garment.

steps.title: Is the oath about what he has or about what he lacks?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the oath should be about the part he owns or about the part he does not own.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does he swear about what he has, or does he swear about what he does not have?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the strange negative wording of the משנה's oath. An oath should state what a person owns, not what he lacks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'I do not have less than half' is odd. It could even be read as 'I have nothing in it.' The question is whether the oath really affirms his ownership or only denies something.
steps.confusionAlert: The question is not how much he owns. It is about how the oath is worded: positive ('I have') or negative ('I don't have less than').

phrases.english: Does he swear about what he has,
or does he swear about what he does not have?!

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל דְּאִית לֵיהּ מִשְׁתְּבַע אוֹ עַל דְּלֵית לֵיהּ מִשְׁתְּבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording quoted in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the oath should affirm what he owns or deny what he does not own.
steps.kashyaTarget: The negative wording of the משנה's oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An oath should affirm ownership, and the negative wording is unclear.

steps.title: רב הונא: he swears both that he has a share and that it is not less than half
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא explains that the oath combines both parts: 'I have a share in it, and I do not have less than half.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: he says, 'An oath that I have a share in it, and I do not have less than half of it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers the question by including both wordings in the oath. First the holder states that he owns part of the garment, then that his part is not less than half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The positive part ('I have in it') makes clear that he is claiming ownership. The negative part ('not less than half') sets the size of his claim. Together they remove the unclear reading of the משנה's short wording.

keyTerms.meaning: I have a share in it

steps.whatToRemember: The oath in שנים אוחזין has two parts: 'I have a share in it,' and 'I do not have less than half of it.'
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the actual wording of the oath used in cases where two people hold an item, and makes the oath clearly about real ownership.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said: he says:
An oath that I have a share in it
and I do not have less than half of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא, דְּאָמַר: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִי בָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The oath includes both: 'I have a share in it' and 'I do not have less than half of it.'

steps.title: Why not swear that all of it is mine?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב הונא's wording: each holder claims the whole טלית, so let him simply swear that all of it is his.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him say: I swear that all of it is mine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב הונא's complicated oath. It suggests a simpler one that matches exactly what the holder is claiming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, each person says 'all of it is mine.' So the natural oath would back up that exact claim. Why invent a new, complicated wording?

keyTerms.meaning: But let him say. Used to suggest a simpler option.

phrases.english: But let him say: an oath that all of it is mine.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנֵימָא שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁכּוּלָּהּ שֶׁלִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's oath wording from step 8
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The oath should match the claim, and the claim is 'all of it is mine.'

steps.title: We would not give him all of it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that he would not get the whole טלית anyway, so it makes no sense to have him swear to that.
steps.simpleTranslation: And do we give him all of it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a question back. Since בית דין will only give him half, an oath about all of it doesn't fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath should match what the person is actually getting. Each holder only walks away with half. So swearing 'all of it is mine' would be pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: And do...? A question that expects the answer 'no'.

phrases.english: And do we give him all of it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי יָהֲבִינַן לֵיהּ כּוּלַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 9
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical outcome: the oath must match what he receives
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The oath should match his full claim
steps.terutzMaskana: The oath should match the half he actually gets

steps.title: Why not swear that half of it is mine?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: if he only gets half, let him simply swear that half is his.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him say: I swear that half of it is mine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another simpler oath. It matches what he actually gets, which is half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said the oath should match the half he receives. So why not swear plainly on half? Why do we need רב הונא's two-part wording?

keyTerms.meaning: That half of it is mine

phrases.english: But let him say: an oath that half of it is mine.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנֵימָא שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁחֶצְיָהּ שֶׁלִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 10's answer to suggest a different simple oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the oath should match what he gets, a plain 'half is mine' is enough.

steps.title: Swearing on half would weaken his own claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that swearing 'half is mine' would go against his original claim that all of it is his.
steps.simpleTranslation: That would damage his own words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the plain 'half' oath doesn't work. It would contradict what he said at first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He told בית דין 'all of it is mine.' If he now swears 'half is mine,' he looks like he is taking back his claim. So neither simple oath works, and that is why רב הונא combined them.

phrases.english: He damages his own statement.
phrases.notes: His 'statement' is his first claim in the משנה: 'all of it is mine.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מַרַע לֵיהּ לְדִיבּוּרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 11
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A plain 'half is mine' oath would be fine
steps.terutzMaskana: It would contradict his claim of 'all of it'

steps.title: רב הונא's wording also weakens his claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: רב הונא's oath ('not less than half') also sounds like he only claims half.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now too, he damages his own statement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the same argument against רב הונא's oath. That oath also seems to back down from 'all of it.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Swearing 'I have not less than half' still sounds like a claim to only half. So the problem from step 12 seems to hit רב הונא's wording too.

phrases.english: Now too, he damages his own statement.
phrases.notes: 'Now' means with רב הונא's wording, the one we are defending.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא נָמֵי מַרַע לֵיהּ לְדִיבּוּרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses step 12's reasoning against רב הונא's wording
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Not less than half' also sounds like he is backing down from 'all of it.'

steps.title: He says: all is mine, but by your terms I swear
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that he keeps his claim to all of it. He only swears on בית דין's terms that he has a share, and not less than half.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he says: All of it is mine. But according to your words, I swear that I have a share in it, and I do not have less than half of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows how רב הונא's wording keeps his claim alive. He says out loud that all of it is his, and swears only within what בית דין will give him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'I have a share in it' don't limit his claim. And 'not less than half' is framed as swearing on בית דין's terms, not as his own claim. So he never takes back 'all of it is mine.'

keyTerms.meaning: According to your words (בית דין's ruling)
I have a share in it

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא's oath does two jobs at once. It keeps the claim to all of the טלית, and it fits the half that בית דין will actually give.

phrases.english: For he says: All of it is mine,
but according to your words, an oath that I have a share in it
phrases.notes: He is talking to the judges: since you'll only give me half, I'll swear on your terms.

phrases.english: and I do not have less than half of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר: כּוּלָּהּ שֶׁלִּי, וּלְדִבְרֵיכֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 and closes the defense of רב הונא's wording
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifying how the oath is phrased
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא's oath backs down from the claim of 'all of it'
steps.terutzMaskana: He states 'all is mine' and swears only on בית דין's terms

steps.title: Why is there an oath at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: since each one is holding the טלית and each keeps his half anyway, what is the oath for?
steps.simpleTranslation: But since this one is holding on and that one is holding on, why is there this oath?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now opens a new question. It is no longer about the wording of the oath. It asks why there is any oath in the first place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both people are holding the טלית, so the outcome is a split no matter what. The oath doesn't seem to change anything. So why make them swear?

phrases.english: But since this one is standing and holding on
and that one is standing and holding on,
why this oath?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁזֶּה תָּפוּס וְעוֹמֵד וְזֶה תָּפוּס וְעוֹמֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the wording of the oath to whether an oath is needed at all
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's requirement of an oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each keeps what he holds anyway, so the oath seems to accomplish nothing.

steps.title: The oath is a rabbinic enactment against grabbing
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that the oath is a תקנת חכמים, so people won't grab someone else's טלית and say 'it's mine.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: This oath is an enactment of the Sages, so that not everyone will go and grab his friend's garment and say, 'It is mine.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן explains that the oath is not required by the תורה. The חכמים added it to stop people from grabbing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without an oath, anyone could grab someone else's טלית, say 'it's mine,' and get half for free. Having to take an oath scares off people who would lie. So the oath protects owners, even though both holders still split the טלית.

keyTerms.meaning: An enactment made by the Sages

steps.whatToRemember: The oath in שנים אוחזין is a תקנת חכמים. It stops people from grabbing what isn't theirs, because a liar won't want to swear.
steps.confusionAlert: The oath does not decide who wins. Both still split the טלית. The oath is only there to scare off people who would grab and lie.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the whole reason for the oath in the משנה. Knowing it is rabbinic, and not from the תורה, matters for later discussions of its rules.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
This oath is an enactment of the Sages,
so that not every single person will
go and grab hold of his fellow's garment
and say: 'It is mine.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: שְׁבוּעָה זוֹ תַּקָּנַת חֲכָמִים הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 15's question about why there is an oath
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the purpose of a rabbinic enactment
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The oath accomplishes nothing because both split anyway
steps.terutzMaskana: The oath is a תקנת חכמים to stop people from grabbing others' property

steps.title: Why trust the oath of someone who may be a thief?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if one of the two holders is falsely grabbing the טלית, he is suspected about money. So he should also be suspected about swearing falsely.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us say: since he is suspected about money, he is also suspected about oaths.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the whole idea of making these two people swear. One of them is likely lying about the טלית, so why believe his oath?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the טלית case, at least one person is claiming something that isn't his, which makes him a suspected thief. The גמרא suggests a מיגו: if he is willing to take money that isn't his, he is probably also willing to swear falsely. If so, his oath is worthless.

keyTerms.meaning: Since / because of (here: 'since he is X, he is also Y')

phrases.english: But let us say: since he is suspected about money,
phrases.notes: He means the one who is grabbing the טלית even though it isn't really his.

phrases.english: he is also suspected about oaths?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנֵימָא מִיגּוֹ דַּחֲשִׁיד אַמָּמוֹנָא חֲשִׁיד נָמֵי אַשְּׁבוּעָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the oath that רבי יוחנן just explained as a תקנת חכמים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The oath given to the two people holding the טלית.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone willing to take money falsely should also be assumed willing to swear falsely, so his oath proves nothing.

steps.title: Suspected about money is not suspected about oaths
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we do not make this jump. A person might take money dishonestly and still be afraid to swear falsely.
steps.simpleTranslation: We do not say that since he is suspected about money he is suspected about oaths.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by rejecting the מיגו. Being dishonest about money does not mean a person will lie under oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Swearing falsely is a much more serious sin than taking money, and even a dishonest person usually treats it that way. So the oath still works as a real check on the person grabbing the טלית.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not say (we do not apply this reasoning)

steps.whatToRemember: Being suspected about money does not automatically make someone suspected about oaths.

phrases.english: We do not say that since he is suspected about money
he is suspected about oaths.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא אָמְרִינַן מִיגּוֹ דַּחֲשִׁיד אַמָּמוֹנָא חֲשִׁיד אַשְּׁבוּעָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the assumed principle (the מיגו) behind the question.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Dishonesty about money spreads to oaths, so the oath is useless.
steps.terutzMaskana: Dishonesty about money does not spread to oaths, so the oath is meaningful.

steps.title: Proof from the oath of one who admits part of a claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to prove the answer: the תורה makes a מודה מקצת הטענה swear. If money-suspicion meant oath-suspicion, that oath would make no sense either.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you don't say so, then about what the תורה says, 'one who admits part of the claim must swear,' let us say: since he is suspected about money, he is suspected about oaths.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof for its answer from a law of the תורה. The תורה trusts the oath of someone who admits part of a debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מודה מקצת הטענה is denying part of what the lender claims, so he looks like someone lying about money. Yet the תורה still makes him swear, which shows the תורה trusts his oath. That would only make sense if money-suspicion does not carry over to oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: For if you don't say so (introduces a proof)
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
One who admits part of the claim against him

phrases.english: For if you don't say so,
then about what the Torah says,
'one who admits part of the claim must swear,'
let us say: since he is suspected about money
he is suspected about oaths.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי לָא תֵּימָא הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 18 with a Torah law.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that money-suspicion does not mean oath-suspicion.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The Torah's oath for a מודה מקצת הטענה.

steps.title: That borrower is only stalling, not stealing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The one who admits part of a loan is not a thief; he is just buying time, as רבה explained.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he is just putting him off, like רבה said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from step 19. The borrower who admits part is not really suspected about money at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrower who denies part of a debt usually plans to pay it all back later. He just doesn't have the money now, so he is stalling. Since he is not a real thief, his case can't teach us about someone who is truly suspected about money.

keyTerms.meaning: He is just slipping away / putting off payment

steps.confusionAlert: This does not cancel the answer of step 18. It only says the proof from מודה מקצת doesn't work, because that borrower is a staller, not a thief.

phrases.english: There, he is just putting him off,
phrases.notes: "There" means the case of the borrower who admits part of the loan.

phrases.english: like רבה said.
phrases.notes: This points to רבה's explanation from earlier in the מסכתא: a borrower who denies part is really just buying time.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם אִשְׁתְּמוֹטֵי קָא מִשְׁתְּמִיט לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from מודה מקצת הטענה, not the principle itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The borrower in that case is not truly suspected about money; he is only stalling.

steps.title: Denying a loan versus denying a deposit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא backs up the difference between stalling and stealing with רב חסדא's rule: one who denies a loan can still be a witness, but one who denies a deposit cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so, for רב אידי בר אבין said in the name of רב חסדא: one who denies a loan is fit to be a witness; one who denies a deposit is unfit to be a witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for the idea from step 20 that a borrower is only stalling. It quotes a rule that treats a lying borrower differently from someone lying about a deposit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A loan is meant to be spent, so a borrower who denies it is assumed to be stalling until he can pay, and he is not called a thief. A deposit may not be used, so someone who denies having it has really taken it, and he is called a thief. That is why only he loses the right to be a witness.

keyTerms.meaning: A deposit left with someone for safekeeping
Fit to serve as a witness

steps.whatToRemember: A borrower who denies a loan is treated as someone stalling, not a thief. Someone who denies a deposit is treated as a thief.
steps.whyThisMatters: This difference between a borrower and someone holding a deposit is a key idea for deciding who is a real thief and who can still be a witness.

phrases.aramaic: תִּדַּע דְּאָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין
phrases.english: Know that this is so, for רב אידי בר אבין said
that רב חסדא said:
One who denies a loan is fit to be a witness.
phrases.notes: He means witnesses showed he was lying, and still he isn't treated as a thief.

phrases.english: One who denies a deposit is unfit to be a witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּדַּע דְּאָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the דחיה of step 20 that a borrower is only stalling.
steps.raayaObject: The difference between stalling on a loan and stealing a deposit.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב חסדא's rule, quoted by רב אידי בר אבין, about who stays fit to be a witness.

steps.title: Why do the four guardians swear if they are thieves?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests the מיגו idea (suspected about money means suspected about oaths) using רמי בר חמא's ברייתא, which makes all four שומרים swear when they admit part of a claim, even though by רב חסדא's rule a שומר cannot claim to be stalling.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about רמי בר חמא's teaching: all four kinds of guardians must swear only when they deny part and admit part. These are the שומר חנם, the שואל, the נושא שכר and the שוכר. Let us say: since he is suspected about money, he is suspected about the oath too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries again to prove that we do not say מיגו דחשיד אממונא חשיד אשבועתא. The borrower's oath was explained as stalling, so now it brings רמי בר חמא's ברייתא, which makes שומרים swear too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא's rule shows that denying a פקדון is treated as stealing, not stalling, so the excuse used for the borrower in step 20 does not seem to fit a שומר. Yet the ברייתא still has a שומר who admits part take an oath, so his oath is trusted. That is hard for anyone who says suspicion about money carries over to oaths.

keyTerms.meaning: Guardians who watch someone else's property
Denying part of the claim and admitting part

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא הָא דְּתָנֵי רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא:
phrases.english: But that which Rami bar Chama taught:
Four guardians require
denial of part and admission of part
the unpaid guardian and the borrower,
the paid guardian and the renter,
let us say: since he is suspected about money,
he is suspected about the oath!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָא דְּתָנֵי רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 20 deflected the proof from the borrower, this uses רב חסדא's distinction from step 21 to bring a new case, the guardians, against the מיגו view of step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion of step 17 that one suspected about money is also suspected about oaths
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A שומר who denies part of a פקדון cannot be called a staller, because רב חסדא treats denying a deposit as theft. If money-suspicion meant oath-suspicion, his oath would be worthless. Yet רמי בר חמא's ברייתא makes him swear.

steps.title: The guardian may also just be stalling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the שומר is not necessarily a thief. He may be buying time to catch the thief or find the lost item.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, he is just stalling. He thinks: I will find the thief and grab it from him. Or: I will find it in the marsh and bring it back to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by showing that the guardian, like the borrower, can be someone buying time and not a thief.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, only the borrower seemed to have the excuse of buying time. Now the גמרא shows that a guardian can also be honestly stalling, since the item was stolen or lost and he hopes to get it back. So he is not a thief, and his oath can be trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: He is just stalling or slipping away for now

phrases.english: There too,
phrases.notes: "There" means the guardian case, just like the borrower in step 20.

phrases.english: he is just stalling.
He thinks: I will find the thief
and grab it from him.
Or else: I will find it in the marsh
and bring it back to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 22
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extends the 'buying time' explanation from the borrower to the guardian
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A guardian who denies a פקדון must be a thief, so his oath is worthless
steps.terutzMaskana: A guardian may be stalling while he tries to recover a stolen or lost item, so he is not a thief and can swear

steps.title: Then why is the denier of a deposit ever disqualified?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the answer around: if a guardian can always be stalling, רב חסדא's rule that the כופר בפקדון is פסול לעדות makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why is one who denies a deposit disqualified from testimony? Let us say he is stalling, thinking: until I search and find it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own answer. The new 'stalling' idea seems to cancel רב חסדא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 23 said a guardian who denies a פקדון may only be buying time. But then every כופר בפקדון could say the same. So when would רב חסדא's rule that he is פסול לעדות ever apply?

keyTerms.meaning: One who denies receiving a deposit
Not allowed to be a witness

phrases.english: If so,
why is one who denies a deposit disqualified from testimony?
phrases.notes: This is רב חסדא's rule from step 21.

phrases.english: Let us say: he is just stalling,
thinking: until I search and find it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 23 by showing it clashes with רב חסדא's rule
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 23 together with רב חסדא's rule in step 21
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If any denier of a deposit may be stalling, no denier of a deposit should ever be treated as a thief who is פסול לעדות.

steps.title: Disqualified only when he clearly had the item
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits רב חסדא's rule to a case where witnesses show the deposit was in his house and he knew it, or he was holding it.
steps.simpleTranslation: When we say one who denies a deposit is disqualified from testimony, it is for example where witnesses came and testified that at that very time the deposit was in his house and he knew it, or that he was holding it in his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing רב חסדא's rule to a case where stalling is impossible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the item was in his house and he knew it, or it was in his hand, he cannot claim he was searching for it. His denial is plain stealing, so he is פסול לעדות. In a normal case, he may be stalling, so he can still swear.
steps.whatToRemember: A שומר who denies a פקדון is usually treated as someone buying time, so he can still swear. He is a thief and פסול לעדות only when witnesses prove he had the item with him and knew it while he denied it.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not cancel רב חסדא's rule. It only limits it to cases where the denier clearly could not have been stalling.

phrases.english: When we say
one who denies a deposit is disqualified from testimony,
it is for example where witnesses came
and testified about him
that at that very time
phrases.notes: The time when he denied it in court.

phrases.english: the deposit was in his house
and he knew it,

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי דַּהֲוָה נָקֵיט לֵיהּ בִּידֵיהּ.
phrases.english: or that he was holding it in his hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the rule to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב חסדא's rule seems to apply to every denier of a deposit, which clashes with the stalling answer
steps.terutzMaskana: רב חסדא's rule applies only when the item was clearly with him and known to him, so stalling is impossible
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the line between a שומר who may still swear and one who is treated as a thief and loses his trust as a witness.

steps.title: Why does רב הונא let a suspected guardian swear?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule 'suspected about money means suspected about oaths' using רב הונא's ruling. רב הונא makes a guardian swear that the item is not in his possession.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about רב הונא's rule? He said we make the guardian swear that the item is not in his possession. Shouldn't we say that since he is suspected about money, he is also suspected about oaths?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new difficulty. רב הונא makes a guardian swear that the item is not with him, even though the reason for the oath is that we suspect he kept it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב הונא's case the guardian says the item is lost and offers to pay. We still make him swear, because we worry he really wants to keep it. That is strange: if we suspect him of keeping someone else's item, the rule 'suspected about money means suspected about oaths' should mean his oath is worth nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Suspected about money (of being dishonest with money)

steps.confusionAlert: The guardian in רב הונא's case is offering to pay. The oath is not about whether he pays. It is about whether he secretly still has the item.

phrases.english: But that which רב הונא said:
we make him swear an oath that it is not in his possession,
let us say: since he is suspected about money,
he is suspected about an oath!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָא דְּאָמַר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב הונא's ruling to test whether a guardian who may be keeping an item can still be trusted with an oath.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion of step 17 that one suspected about money is also suspected about oaths, tested against רב הונא's rule that a guardian who offers to pay must swear the item is not in his possession
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The oath exists because we suspect him of keeping the item. Someone suspected about money is suspected about oaths, so the oath should be useless.

steps.title: He tells himself that paying makes it fine
steps.stepSummary: The guardian is not a real thief in his own eyes. He convinces himself it is allowed because he is paying for the item.
steps.simpleTranslation: There too, he tells himself it is permitted and says: 'I am giving him money for it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the guardian who keeps the item does not see himself as stealing. He thinks paying for it makes it okay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who is ready to swear falsely is a person who knowingly takes money that isn't his. This guardian honestly thinks he did nothing wrong, since the owner gets paid. So he is not suspected about oaths, and his oath can be trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: Rules for himself, convinces himself it is permitted
Money, payment (the value of the item)

phrases.english: There too, he rules for himself and says:
'I am giving him money.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם נָמֵי, מוֹרֶה וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רב הונא by explaining that the guardian does not see himself as a thief.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the person's mindset: he is not knowingly dishonest
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Anyone who keeps an item that isn't his is a thief and can't be trusted to swear.
steps.terutzMaskana: A guardian who pays for the item thinks he did nothing wrong, so he is not suspected of swearing falsely.

steps.title: But paying still breaks לא תחמוד
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדיפתי asks רבינא: even if the guardian pays, taking an item the owner wants back breaks the לאו of לא תחמוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא from דיפתי said to רבינא: But he is still breaking the לאו of 'You shall not covet'!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא מדיפתי pushes back on the last answer. Paying does not make it permitted, because forcing someone to give up his item breaks לא תחמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 27 depended on the guardian doing nothing wrong in his own eyes. רב אחא points out that the Torah forbids taking something from its owner against his will even if you pay. So the guardian really is doing an איסור, and we are back to doubting his oath.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You shall not covet' — the commandment against desiring and taking what belongs to someone else

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּיפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: רב אחא of דיפתי said to רבינא:

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא קָא עָבַר עַל לָאו דְּ״לֹא תַּחְמֹד״?
phrases.english: But isn't he breaking the prohibition of 'You shall not covet'?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא קָא עָבַר עַל לָאו דְּ״לֹא תַּחְמֹד״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 27 by showing that paying does not make keeping the item permitted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a guardian who pays thinks he is doing nothing wrong
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Taking someone's item against his will, even with payment, breaks לא תחמוד. So the guardian is knowingly sinning and should be suspected about oaths.

steps.title: People think לא תחמוד means taking without paying
steps.stepSummary: Most people understand לא תחמוד as forbidding only taking without paying. So the guardian does not realize he is sinning.
steps.simpleTranslation: People understand 'You shall not covet' to mean taking something without paying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ordinary people don't know that לא תחמוד applies even when you pay. They think it only covers taking for free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא accepts that the guardian technically breaks לא תחמוד. What matters for trusting his oath is his own mindset, and he does not know he is doing wrong. Someone who sins without knowing it is not the kind of person we suspect of swearing falsely.

keyTerms.meaning: It is understood by them, they take it to mean

steps.whatToRemember: A guardian who keeps an item and pays for it is still trusted to swear. Most people think לא תחמוד only means taking without paying, so he does not see himself as a sinner or a thief.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying לא תחמוד is permitted with payment. It is saying the guardian doesn't know that, so he is not someone we suspect of lying under oath.

phrases.english: 'You shall not covet,' to people,
is understood by them as taking without paying.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״לֹא תַּחְמֹד״ לְאִינָשֵׁי בְּלָא דְּמֵי מַשְׁמַע לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא מדיפתי's challenge and saves the answer of step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Focus on what the person believes, not on the technical איסור
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the guardian breaks לא תחמוד, he is knowingly sinning and can't be trusted to swear.
steps.terutzMaskana: Most people wrongly think לא תחמוד requires taking without payment, so the guardian does not know he is sinning and his oath is still trusted.
